findings.claim: \(g\) is gravitational field strength (10 N/kg on Earth); the worked example, two mark schemes and two flashcards all use g = 10 N/kg.
findings.truth: AQA 8463 uses g = 9.8 N/kg. The spec says a freely falling object near the Earth's surface accelerates at about 9.8 m/s2, and that the value of g is given in any calculation. Recomputed: E_p = 2 x 9.8 x 5 = 98 J, v = 9.9 m/s; 2 x 9.8 x 10 = 196 J (not 200 J, so 'twice' becomes 'about twice'); 500 x 9.8 x 20 = 98 000 J and P = 1960 W.
findings.evidence: spec 4.5.6.1.5 ('an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s2'); spec 4.1.1.3 and 4.5.1.3 (g will be given); recomputation

findings.claim: Cloze answer 'mass / g (gravitational field strength).' for 'Gravitational potential energy = ____ x ____ x height.'
findings.truth: The two blanks are mass and g. Written with a slash inside an equation cloze it reads as mass divided by g, which is a different (wrong) equation.
findings.evidence: spec appendix A equation 11, E_p = m g h

findings.claim: 'Ek = 0.5 x m x v^2 (mass x velocity squared divided by 2).'
findings.truth: The spec words this equation with speed, not velocity. The article body already says speed. Harmless at GCSE, so no edit.
findings.evidence: spec appendix A equation 10 ('kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x speed 2')

findings.claim: A higher-only box gives P = Fv 'for calculating the power output of engines or motors'.
findings.truth: P = Fv is not in the 8463 equation list, on either the recall list or the equation sheet, and no spec statement requires it. It is correct physics and is behind a wrapper, so it is enrichment rather than an error.

findings.claim: 'Reducing Unwanted Energy Transfers' (thermal insulation, lubrication, wall thickness and cooling rate, n15-n18) sits inside <div class="higher-only">.
findings.truth: Spec 4.1.2.1 carries no HT flag: all students must explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfers through lubrication and thermal insulation, and describe how the rate of cooling of a building depends on wall thickness and thermal conductivity. It also underpins required practical 2 (thermal insulation), which every candidate does. Practice question 2 (2 marks, both tiers) asks for two ways to reduce energy loss from a house, so Foundation students are asked about content they cannot see. Only the separate line 'describe ways to increase the efficiency of an intended energy transfer' (4.1.2.2) is HT only, and that already sits unwrapped in the n14 key fact.
findings.evidence: spec 4.1.2.1 (no tier flag) and required practical activity 2; contrast spec 4.1.2.2 '(HT only)'

findings.claim: n27 gives 1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2; n32 gives P = V^2/R.
findings.truth: The spec states that students are not required to calculate the total resistance of two resistors joined in parallel, and P = V^2/R is not in either 8463 equation list. Both are correct physics presented as asides (the parallel formula is already behind a higher-only wrapper), so no edit here; the same formula IS asserted as required recall in lesson 4, which is fixed there.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2.2 ('Students are not required to calculate the total resistance of two resistors joined in parallel'); spec appendix A

findings.claim: The parallel resistance formula is taught as required: n14 introduces it as how total parallel resistance 'is found', the Key Takeaways list it as a headline equation, and a flashcard asks 'What equation gives total resistance of two resistors in parallel?'
findings.truth: AQA 8463 states plainly that students are not required to calculate the total resistance of two resistors joined in parallel. Students must only explain qualitatively why parallel resistance falls below the smallest branch. Keeping the algebra as clearly-labelled extension is fine; presenting it as an examinable recall item is not.

findings.claim: The practical box is titled 'Required Practical: I-V Characteristics' with no number.
findings.truth: On 8463 the I-V characteristics investigation is required practical activity 4 (activity 3 is resistance). The number is what students revise by, and this unit is the separate-physics build, so Trilogy numbering must not be inherited.
findings.evidence: spec 8.2.4 'Required practical activity 4: ... investigate the I-V characteristics of a variety of circuit elements'

findings.claim: 'The UK mains supply is alternating current (a.c.) at about 230 V and a frequency of 50 Hz. This means the current changes direction 50 times per second.'
findings.truth: 50 Hz means 50 complete cycles per second. Each cycle reverses the current twice, so the current changes direction 100 times per second, not 50. This is a classic misconception stated here as fact.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2.3.1 (50 Hz, about 230 V); definition of frequency as cycles per second

findings.claim: The whole National Grid section (n24-n26: high-voltage transmission, P = I^2 R losses, step-up and step-down transformers) sits inside <div class="higher-only">.
findings.truth: Spec 4.2.4.3 carries no tier flag: all students must know the grid is cables and transformers, that step-up transformers raise the potential difference for transmission and step-down transformers lower it for domestic use, and must explain why this is efficient. Only the construction and operation of transformers (topic 7, Paper 2) is HT only. The lesson's own exam tip and practice question 4 (3 marks) already assume this content at both tiers.
findings.evidence: spec 4.2.4.3 (no tier flag; 'The construction and operation of transformers is covered Transformers (HT only)')

findings.claim: Circuit breaker is defined (in the dfn data-def and in the glossary) as 'An automatic switch that breaks a circuit when it detects a difference between the live and neutral currents.'
findings.truth: That is a residual current device. A circuit breaker breaks the circuit when the current rises above a set value, doing the fuse's job, and can be reset. The lesson's own prose says it 'does the same job but can be reset', so the definition contradicts the sentence it sits in.
findings.evidence: settled fact; spec 4.2.3.2 (mains safety); the lesson's own n10 sentence

findings.claim: The dfn on 'mass' carries data-def='The amount of substance in a given volume.'
findings.truth: That is the definition of density, the very quantity the paragraph is about. Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. ('Amount of substance' is also the chemistry quantity measured in moles.) A student who hovers the term is taught the circular wrong definition.
findings.evidence: spec 4.3.1.1 (density = mass / volume; mass, m, in kilograms)

findings.claim: Practice question 5 is typed '9 marks - Evaluate' with a Top band (7-9) / Mid band (4-6) / Lower band (1-3) ladder.
findings.truth: AQA 8463 has no 9-mark question. Both papers are 1 hour 45 minutes and 100 marks, built from multiple choice, structured, closed short answer and open response items; extended response items run to 6 marks. A 9-mark ladder trains the wrong answer length.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments (Paper 1 and Paper 2: 1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks, question types listed)

findings.claim: Practice question 6 is typed '12 marks - Extended Response'.
findings.truth: Same error, larger. There is no 12-mark item on either 8463 paper; 6 marks is the extended-response ceiling.

findings.claim: 'Particle Model Explanation' (n26-n32: how melting, boiling, condensing and freezing change particle arrangement and forces) sits inside <div class="higher-only">.
findings.truth: Spec 4.3.1.1, 4.3.1.2 and 4.3.2 carry no tier flags. All students must use the particle model to explain the differences between solids, liquids and gases and the changes of state. Practice questions 2 and 5 (both tiers) test exactly this, so Foundation students are examined on hidden content.

findings.claim: Three <div class="higher-only"> wrappers hide the properties of alpha, beta and gamma radiation (n10-n12), the half-life fractions and the worked half-life calculation (n15-n18), and contamination versus irradiation (n21-n22).
findings.truth: None of this is HT only. Spec 4.4.2.1 (nature, range and penetration of alpha, beta and gamma), 4.4.2.3 (half-life, and the net decline as a ratio) and 4.4.2.4 (contamination and irradiation) carry no tier flags. With the wrappers in place a Foundation student sees only the names of the three radiations and a one-line half-life definition, yet practice questions 2, 3 and 5 and the exam tip test the hidden material at both tiers.

findings.claim: 'In 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and proposed the plum pudding model'.
findings.truth: Thomson identified the electron in 1897; the plum pudding model followed in 1904. The sentence reads as though both happened in 1897. No date is required by the spec and no mark turns on it, so no edit.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1.3 (the discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model; no dates required)

findings.claim: Lesson 2 description is 103 characters and lesson 4 description is 100 characters.
findings.truth: The house validator rejects a lesson description of 100 characters or more, so the whole unit would fail on write. Not a fact error, but it blocks every other fix in this unit from landing. Trimmed to 96 and 99 characters with no change of meaning.
findings.evidence: house validator limit; measured lengths 103 and 100

findings.claim: The unit is the eight Combined-Science physics lessons unchanged. It carries no separate-physics-only Paper 1 content at all.
findings.truth: 8463 Paper 1 is topics 1-4 and includes separate-only material this unit omits entirely: static electricity and electric fields (4.2.5.1, 4.2.5.2); the whole particle model and pressure section (4.3.3.1 particle motion in gases, 4.3.3.2 pV = constant, 4.3.3.3 doing work on a gas, HT only); background radiation and radiation dose (4.4.3.1); different half-lives and their uses (4.4.3.2, 4.4.3.3); and nuclear fission and fusion (4.4.4). Two core both-qualification items are also absent: mass number, atomic number and isotopes (4.4.1.2) and nuclear equations (4.4.2.2). The sibling unit science-aqa/physics-paper-1 carries lessons 9 (Static Electricity and Electric Fields), 10 (Gas Pressure and Pressure in Fluids) and 11 (Nuclear Radiation: Uses, Fission and Fusion) - separate-only content sitting in the Combined build, where it does not belong. Options: (a) move or rebuild those three lessons into this unit and drop them from science-aqa, then add isotopes and nuclear equations; (b) leave the split and accept that separate-physics students revise Paper 1 from an incomplete unit. Recommendation: (a). Note that lesson 10 also carries pressure in fluids, which is 4.5.5 and therefore Paper 2, so it must be split when moved.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 (Paper 1 = topics 1-4); spec 4.2.5, 4.3.3, 4.4.3, 4.4.4 (all marked physics only); spec 4.4.1.2 and 4.4.2.2; scripts/_retrofc/units/science-aqa__physics-paper-1/_brief.json

summary: One hard error (50 Hz taught as 50 direction changes a second) and a systematic tier fault: five higher-only wrappers across lessons 2, 5, 7 and 8 hide both-tier core content (insulation, the National Grid, the particle model of state change, alpha/beta/gamma properties, half-life calculation, contamination versus irradiation) that the same lessons then examine at both tiers. Also g taught as 10 N/kg where 8463 uses 9.8, two definitions that describe the wrong quantity, a 9-mark and a 12-mark question on a board whose ceiling is 6, and the parallel-resistance formula taught as required recall when the spec excludes it. Unit-level: this is the Combined build unchanged and carries none of the separate-only Paper 1 content.
